title: The family of relational structures, and which choice each one makes

what.formal: A relational structure is fixed by independent modelling choices: the maximum arity of a relation (2, or unbounded); whether relations are directed; whether two objects may be related more than once, and with what weight; and whether the objects fall into distinct kinds that may only relate across kinds. A structure is named by which of these it relaxes.
what.plain: There is more than one way to record who is related to whom, and each way makes a different compromise. Picking the right one is a modelling decision, not a notation preference.

head: Structure
What it relaxes
Canonical example
rows: who follows whom; who cites whom
several distinct flights between two cities
users and the films they rated
authors and the papers they co-wrote

what.md: These choices are independent, which is why the family is a grid rather than a ladder: you can have a weighted directed hypergraph, and the literature contains such things. **A hypergraph is not a more advanced graph; it is a graph that has given up the arity restriction.** It makes no claim about direction, weights or kinds.

This paper treats several genuinely directed relations — citations in Cora, follows in Github — as undirected. That is a deliberate simplification inherited from the datasets' standard usage, and it is not the same decision as using a hypergraph. When Chapter 7 asks what the paper does not address, direction is one of the items worth remembering.

example.md: **Example 1 — one dataset, five structures.** Take a music streaming service with users and songs, where each user has several listening sessions, and each session is a list of songs played in order.

items: **Bipartite graph** — users on one side, songs on the other, a link for each play. Good for "who listens to what"; it treats users and songs as different kinds of thing.
**Ordinary graph on songs** — link two songs if one user played them back to back. Every link is a pair, so a 30-song session becomes 29 links and the session is gone.
**Directed graph on songs** — the same links with an arrow. Preserves order, still loses the session.
**Weighted graph on songs** — weight each link by how often that transition happens. Preserves frequency, still loses the session.
**Hypergraph on songs** — one hyperedge per session, containing every song played in it. Preserves the session as a unit; loses the order *within* the session.

example.md: Notice that no structure wins outright: the hypergraph preserves the group but discards the ordering, and a directed graph does the reverse. **The right question is never "which structure is better" but "which property of my data do I refuse to lose"** — and then checking that the method you pick does not quietly require the property you sacrificed.

quiz.q: Which restriction does a hypergraph relax, relative to an ordinary graph?

opts.expl: Hypergraphs are also undirected — a hyperedge is a set, and sets have no order. Direction is relaxed by directed graphs, a different member of the family.

opts.md: That a relation must involve exactly two objects
opts.expl: Correct — arity, and only arity. A hypergraph says nothing about weights, direction or kinds, which is why those remain separate choices you may still have to make.

opts.md: That two objects may be related only once
opts.expl: That restriction is relaxed by multigraphs. In fact a hypergraph can express multiplicity differently — two distinct hyperedges with the same membership — which is why the family's choices are best treated as independent rather than stacked.

quiz.q: A dataset has 40 listening sessions, with 15 songs in each on average. How many hyperedges does the session-based hypergraph have?
quiz.hint: One hyperedge per session — do not multiply by the songs.
quiz.sol: 40 hyperedges, each of size about 15. Multiplying to get 600 would be counting *memberships*, which is the sum of the column sums, not the number of hyperedges. The two quantities are the two degrees again: 600 memberships over however many distinct songs there are gives the average vertex degree.

quiz.q: A dataset records that Alice follows Bob, but Bob does not follow Alice. Which structure records this without loss?

opts.expl: An ordinary graph's edges are symmetric: recording Alice–Bob automatically asserts Bob–Alice, which is false here.

Correct. Direction is exactly the property being lost, and it is relaxed by adding arrows — not by allowing larger groups. The paper's Github dataset is a follow network used as if undirected; that is a modelling simplification worth remembering when you read its results.
A hyperedge would let you name the group {Alice, Bob}, but it could not say which way the follow points. Larger arity does not buy direction.

close: **Where this is going:** having chosen the hypergraph, there are still two equivalent ways to write one down. Card 3 gives both, and shows why the matrix version is the one that ends up in the paper's equations.
